author: Andy Coughlan
title: 'Ugly Lies the Bone' addresses wounded vet's homecoming - NewsBreak
text:
By Andy Coughlan ,
10 hours ago Nick Lopez, left, Shelby Eason and Gracie Parsley rehearse a scene for "Ugly Lies the Bone" in Lamar University's Studio Theatre. The play runs Sept. 25 to 28. (Photo by Andy Coughlan) Jess returns to her Florida home after her third tour of Afghanistan badly scarred from severe burns. But the world she returns to is different from that which she remembers.
Not only does she look and feel different, but the way people react to her has also changed.
Lindsey Ferrentino’s “Ugly Lies the Bone,” presented Sept. 25 to 28 in Lamar University’s Studio Theatre, follows Jess and her family and friends as they navigate the changed relationships to each other.
“How do you move forward with your life when confronted with all these changes that are happening,” director Alan Brincks said.
Ferrentino incorporates a virtual reality system created to help burn victims into the plot, Brincks said.
“Your skin's peeled off and burned off, essentially, and all your nerve endings are exposed, so they came up with this VR program specifically for burn victims, originally in the military, called Snow World,” Brincks said. “You could go in and it just short circuits your brain and allows your brain to focus on something else while you're doing the physical therapy.”
As Jess receives her therapy, she is seen in different environments.
“We go back and forth between places that she grew up in and this virtual world that is being built for her, around her,” Brincks said.
Gracie Parsley plays Jess, who she said is a complex character.
“Who she is in the story that y'all hear is vastly different from who she has been her whole life and all the trauma she's endured,” Parsley said. “She's got a harder shell. And I think that's something about her that people kind of just look over.
“She's been training in the military — enduring, enduring, enduring — and taking all this and just being OK with it. When she comes back to civilian life, she doesn't know how to cope with how things aren't the same as how they used to be.”
Jess is offended by how she is treated, Parsley said. She’s been to war and seen things people can’t imagine and now she finds herself bottom of the pyramid.
“People see her and they're like, ‘Yes, she's been through a lot of physical trauma,’ but I think a good portion of it also is her mental trauma and all the bad she's seen that she can't talk about,” Parsley said.
Porter LaPray plays Stevie, an old boyfriend who split up with Jess shortly before her last tour of duty.
“Stevie's a little bit of goofball,” LaPray said. “He loves to smile, to crack jokes. He's, he's always got to fill that silence, you know, he can't let an awkward moment linger.
“I feel like he's not able to really give Jess what she needs. Jess is in a really tough spot and Stevie's world is not very tough, so it's kind of hard for him to meet her halfway.”
“Ugly Lies the Bone” is thought-provoking and LaPray said every time he has left rehearsal it has hung with him a little heavier.
“Whenever people ask me what this plays about, I say it's a slice-of-life piece about just how terrible war is,” LaPray said. “You think about it in its broad sense, and it's hard to encompass all of what you're seeing on the news. But just picking apart the individual stories and how it affects people when they get back home is just, it's awful.”
Shelby Eason as Jess’ sister Kacie and Nick Lopez as Kelvin round out the ensemble, with Roxy Hamm as the voice the VR.
Parsley said she hopes audiences come to an awareness and understanding of how veterans are not conditioned back into society. Trauma can reveal itself though small things, she said.
“They are just so lost when they return,” she said. “People know that veterans struggle going back into life, but they don't see it. There's a moment in the show where Kelvin is flicking a lighter, or Stevie rings the bell, and it's just an instant (reaction). It's like every day (Jess is) not knowing what to expect, and any little thing can just trigger that.”
Brincks said it's important for the audience to remember that we are all in the world together.
“How do we look at each other's differences and accept them in order to make this world a home for everyone, and not just people that relate to or look like yourself,” he said. “How can we embrace everyone's differences and challenges and everything else, and make it a home for everyone, as opposed to just a few.”
Showtimes are 7:30 p.m., Sept. 25 to 27, and 2 p.m., Sept. 28. General admission tickets are $15, $10 for seniors, $7 for students with Lamar University ID and $5 for children 12 and under. For tickets, visit lamar.edu/lutdtx.
